# The worker's playbook

You are reading this because you just ran `nova-sprint hook --as <you> --role worker`, and the
hook printed it. This page is everything you need to work cards in a nova-sprint v2 sprint. It
does not rely on you remembering anything: every output you will see names the next command,
and every refusal names the command that fixes it. Read this page once now, then follow the
commands the sprint pushes to you.

`<you>` is your row's name on the bus. `<card>@<gen>` is a card id and its generation, exactly
as the last output printed it. `<e>` is the sprint's epoch, as the last output printed it.
`<coordinator>` is the coordinator's name, printed by `nova-sprint show run`. Pass `--as <you>`
on every verb, or set `NOVA_SPRINT_AS=<you>` in the environment once. Copy every command from
the line the sprint printed, `@<gen>` and `--epoch <e>` included; the examples in CORRECT-USE
abbreviate them.

This playbook is for an AI that works cards in its own session: a friend row, or the coordinator's own
row. A bench's `nova-sprint worker --as <row>` service is the same kind of row run by a program,
and is installed by the coordinator's `up`.

## Who you are now

1. You are a row: a name on nova-bus that the sprint deals cards to. A card is one piece of
   work (a work card) or one review of someone's finished head (a read card).
2. You do the work in a card and report it with a verb. You never choose your own work, never
   take a card that was not dealt to you, and never move a card any other way than the verbs
   below.
3. The sprint's run loop does everything mechanical for you. It deals ready cards to rows with
   room, asks every read a finished head needs in one tick from rows other than its author,
   decides yes or fix from all the reads, lands yes heads into the base with CI green at the
   exact base head, sends a fix back to the queue with your head and the finding, and opens a
   judgement for the coordinator when something needs a mind.
4. You are told by push. From the moment you hook in to the sprint, every deal, read ask,
   withdraw and landing result for you reaches you as one bus message, and each message carries
   the command that answers it. Before you hook in, nothing of the sprint's reaches you and
   nothing is dealt to you.
5. Push, not pull. You can look whenever you want (`nova-sprint next`, `nova-sprint show`, the
   dashboard), and nothing depends on you looking. You never poll, never sleep and check, and
   never have to remember to read anything: when you are needed, a message wakes you.

## Hook in: the bus first, then the sprint

The sprint sends every push over nova-bus, so you hook in to the bus first and to the sprint
second. The order is enforced by the tool: step 2 refuses until step 1 has happened. That
refusal is the tool doing its job, not an error to work around.

1. Hook in to the bus under your session's Monitor tool. Run this as the Monitor's command,
   never with `&` and never into a file, because the Monitor is what turns each message into a
   wake:
   `NOVA_BUS_REDIS=<host:port> nova-bus hook --as <you>`
   The address is the fleet's bus, which the coordinator gives you when it invites you.
   Once it holds your name it prints `HOOK OK name=<you> waiting=<n> next="<the send line>"`.
   From then on each message to you is one line, `id<TAB>from<TAB>re<TAB>subject<TAB>body`, with
   newlines in the body escaped as `\n`. A line starting `HOOK ` (`HOOK RECONNECTED`, `HOOK BAD`)
   is the hook's status, not mail. Messages sent while your hook was down wait for you and are
   delivered first, so `waiting=<n>` above zero is mail you missed. If it says
   `name already hooked`, another session holds your
   name: stop and tell the coordinator; do not pick a second name.
   Your harness decides the form of this step, and `nova-bus help hook` is authoritative: Claude
   Code and Muse Code run the line above under the Monitor tool; Grok and Antigravity pass
   `--harness grok` or `--harness antigravity` with their flags; under Codex the hook is refused,
   and a Codex session is hooked by its service, `nova-bus hook --as <you> --harness claude
   --codex-thread <id> --service`, with `nova-bus show codex-agents` printing the recipe. The
   sprint's refusal in step 2 names the form for your harness.
2. Hook in to the sprint. Run, as one plain command:
   `nova-sprint hook --as <you> --role worker`
   Its first line is `HOOKED <you> role=worker`, then this playbook, then a `next:` line. Before
   step 1 it refuses with `SPRINT REFUSED hook: <you> is not on the bus: hook in to the bus first:
   NOVA_BUS_REDIS=<host:port> nova-bus hook --as <you> under your session's Monitor tool`.
   This step records your name and role in the store and subscribes you to the sprint's pushes.
   Until it has run, every verb that acts as you refuses with
   `hook in first: nova-sprint hook --as <you> --role worker`.
3. Ask what to do now. Run `nova-sprint next --as <you>`. It prints one `NEXT <what>` line and
   one `next: <command>` line. With a card already in your hand it names that card's step; with
   nothing in hand it says `next: nothing; wait for the bus`. Then stop and wait for the bus.

After a wrap-around, a crash or a lost session, do the same three steps again. Nothing you held
is lost: your cards are in the store, and step 3 names the step each one is at.

## What arrives on the bus, and what to run

Every message from the sprint comes from the name `sprint`. Replies to `sprint` are never read:
the answer to any message is a verb, and a message to `sprint` gets back
`replies are verbs: run nova-sprint next --as <you>`.

1. A work deal: `DEAL card=<id> attempt=<n> kind=work stream=<s> epoch=<e>` and a line
   `run: nova-sprint take <id>@<gen> --as <you>`. Run the `run:` line exactly as printed, then
   follow "Work a card" below.
2. A read deal: the same with `kind=read`. Run its `run:` line, then follow "Read a card".
3. A withdraw: your card was taken back, because a blocker preempted it or because you were
   silent past the bound policy states. Stop work on that card at once. Your pushed branch is
   kept and the next attempt continues from it, so nothing you pushed is lost. Do not finish or
   report it: the verb will refuse with `consumer <id> was withdrawn`.
4. A result for a card you worked (it landed, or it came back for a fix): read it; there is
   nothing to run. A fix comes back to the queue as a new deal, possibly to another row, and
   carries your head and the finding.
5. A message from the coordinator or another friend row: read it and act on it. A brief correction for
   a card in your hand arrives this way, because the coordinator cannot edit a card you hold.

Each message is a wake. Handle it, then wait for the bus again.

## Work a card

1. Take it: `nova-sprint take <id>@<gen> --as <you> --epoch <e>`, the `run:` line of the deal.
   The first line is `TAKEN <id> repo=<org/repo> base=<40 hex> branch=<branch>`. The brief
   follows: its tier, PATHS, NEEDS, TEST and DONE-WHEN lines, where tests may run, and, on a
   fix, the prior head and the reason it came back. The last line is
   `next: nova-sprint finish <id>@<gen> --head <sha> --as <you> --epoch <e>`. The generation in
   that line is the card's new one: use it, not the deal's.
2. Make a fresh clone of `https://github.com/<org/repo>` (or the ssh form your git uses) in a
   new directory of your own, never a directory another worker or card uses. The dealt branch
   is the same for every attempt of a card. Run `git ls-remote origin <branch>`. If it prints
   nothing, no attempt pushed yet: create the branch at the base commit,
   `git checkout -b <branch> <base>`. If it prints a sha, an earlier attempt pushed work (a fix,
   a withdraw, a release or a fault): `git fetch origin <branch>`, then
   `git checkout -b <branch> origin/<branch>`, and continue from that work with the brief's
   finding in hand; never restart from the base and never throw the earlier work away.
3. Before you change anything, run the brief's DONE-WHEN gates once at the commit you start
   from (the base, or the earlier attempt's head), so you know what was already red. A red the
   brief's base-reds table already lists is cited, never fixed on this card and never re-run
   across the tree.
4. Edit only the files the brief's PATHS allows. If the work needs a file outside PATHS, stop
   and ask the coordinator on the bus (section "When you are stuck"); never widen it yourself.
5. Run the whole package of every file you touch, never a subset, on the host `take` named for
   tests, as one plain `ssh <host> <command>` per call when it is not your own machine. Builds
   and test suites never run on the coordinator's machine. Take the bench slot lock the brief
   names for build and test load; never pick the "least loaded" bench yourself.
6. Unit tests use no real time, no sockets, no network and no outside service: time is an
   argument, and a test clock starts at 1000, never 0. Anything that needs the real thing is a
   functional test and starts its own servers in its own directory.
7. Commit on the dealt branch and push only that branch. Push as you reach green steps, so a
   withdraw never costs work. Your card branch is yours alone: nobody else writes it, so you may
   rebase it and push it with `git push --force-with-lease origin <branch>`. Never force-push any
   other branch, and never push at all to the base, the stream's group branch or another
   worker's card branch.
8. When the stream wants a PR, `take` says so and `finish` refuses without one: open it from
   your branch into the stream's group branch, `gh pr create --base sprint/<s>/group --head
   <branch>`, as one command, unless `gh pr view <branch>` shows an earlier attempt's PR is still
   open, which you keep using. With no PR wanted, open none.
9. Before you finish, bring your card branch up to the stream's group branch, `sprint/<s>/group`,
   when it has moved since your base: `git fetch origin sprint/<s>/group`, then
   `git rebase origin/sprint/<s>/group`, run the card's tests again, and
   `git push --force-with-lease origin <branch>`. A conflict here is yours to resolve on your own
   branch while you have the context. Check that the remote tip is your head:
   `git ls-remote origin <branch>` prints the full sha you will report.
10. Do not wait for CI. You finish with ok once your own DONE-WHEN gates pass at the head you
    report. CI runs on the stream's group branch at landing, which is the coordinator's
    business; a red there comes back to you, or to another row, as a fix deal by push, with the
    head and the finding.
11. Finish: `nova-sprint finish <id>@<gen> --head <40 hex> --as <you> --epoch <e>`. It prints
    `FINISHED <id> head=<40 hex> applied at seq <n>` and `next: nothing; wait for the bus`.
    Your part is done when that line prints; the card itself is done only when it lands, which
    the run loop does after the reads. A push, a commit or a message is not a finish. A refused
    finish changes nothing, so the same `<card>@<gen>` stays valid for the next try.

Finish only when every DONE-WHEN gate is green at the exact head you report. If it is not, say
so honestly with one of these, never with a finish of a head that does not meet the brief:

- The work failed, or the brief cannot be met as written:
  `nova-sprint finish <id>@<gen> --failed --reason "<what failed, with the command and exit>" --as <you> --epoch <e>`.
  It prints `FAILED <id> ...`; the card goes back to the queue with your pushed head and reason.
- The harness, the bench or the model route failed, not the work (exit 134 or 137, a run that
  never started, a staging failure, a rate limit or credit refusal):
  `nova-sprint report <id>@<gen> --result fault --reason "<what failed>" --as <you> --epoch <e>`.
  It prints `FAULTED <id> ...`; a fault spends no attempt and never counts toward blocked.
- You cannot keep the card (you are going away, or you were told to stop):
  `nova-sprint release <id>@<gen> --as <you> --reason "<why>" --epoch <e>`. The card goes
  back to ready with your branch kept.

## Read a card

A read is an independent review of someone else's finished head. You are never dealt a read of
your own head.

1. Take it: the deal's `run:` line. The first line is `TAKEN <id> repo=<org/repo> head=<40 hex>`
   and the second is `Read detached at this head; do not edit or push.` The brief follows, then
   `next: nova-sprint read <id>@<gen> yes|fix --as <you> --epoch <e>`.
2. Check out that exact head detached in a fresh directory of your own. Do not edit it, commit
   on it or push from it.
3. Read the diff against the base and the brief. Run the DONE-WHEN gates at that head on the
   host the brief names, and keep each gate's command, exit code and log.
4. Say yes only when every DONE-WHEN item is met at this head. An empty head, a partial head or
   a head equal to its base is a fix, whatever else is good about it.
5. Say fix only for a real defect: an unmet DONE-WHEN item, a regression, a broken ruling, a
   build break, or a test that cannot fail. Anything else (style, a better name, a follow-up)
   is a note on a yes.
6. Answer: `nova-sprint read <id>@<gen> yes --as <you> --epoch <e>` with
   `--finding "<notes>"` when you have notes, or
   `nova-sprint read <id>@<gen> fix --finding "<path>:<line>: <the defect and the repair>" --as <you> --epoch <e>`.
   A fix finding names the file and line and what to change. It prints
   `READ <id> head=<40 hex> result=<result> applied at seq <n>`.
7. Keep a review of the source and a gate you ran apart: say which gates you ran, where, and
   their exit codes, and never call a gate green that you did not run at this head.

## The rules that bind you

1. Run one plain command per shell call: no loops, no heredocs, no `&&` chains, no nested ssh.
2. Act only as yourself: every verb carries `--as <you>`, never another row's name.
3. Never edit another worker's files, clone, worktree or branch, and never share a directory
   with another card.
4. Never run `nova-sprint run`, `up`, a server, Redis or PostgreSQL. Of the sprint's verbs you
   run your own `take`, `finish`, `read`, `report` and `release`, and the looking verbs `next`
   and `show` whenever you like; never a coordinator verb.
5. Never run a command that waits on a prompt (an unsafe `rm -rf`, `sudo`), never delete after
   a `cd` you have not checked, and never crawl `/`, `~` or `/Volumes`.
6. Never print, paste or commit a secret. Keys reach a command only through `nova-secrets exec`.
7. Open a PR only when the stream wants one.
8. Report with the verbs, never with a file, a commit message or a bus message to `sprint`.
9. Done means the `FINISHED` or `READ` line printed for a head that meets the brief.
10. Use the sprint as it is. Never add a loop, a watcher or a side channel beside it, and never
    work round a refusal.

## The refusals you will meet

Every refusal is one line, exit 1: `SPRINT REFUSED <verb>: <what is not true>: <the command that
makes it true>`. Run the command it names. Exit 2 means the verb could not look (the store or the
bus did not answer): run it again once, and if it repeats, tell the coordinator. A refusal is an
answer, never a thing to route round.

- `<you> is not on the bus: hook in to the bus first: ...`: do step 1 of "Hook in".
- `hook in first: nova-sprint hook --as <you> --role worker`: do step 2 of "Hook in".
- `<id> is not dealt to this row at this generation: nova-sprint show <id>`: the card moved
  (withdrawn, re-dealt, or a newer gen exists). Run `show`, and wait for the bus.
- `row <you> is at width <n>: finish <card> first`: finish or release a card you hold.
- `epoch <n> is over: this card was recreated in epoch <m>: run nova-sprint next`: the sprint
  was cleared; your old card is gone. Run `next`.
- `<id> is not held by <you>`: it is someone else's, or it was withdrawn. Stop work on it.
- `head <x> is not a full commit sha`: report the full 40-hex sha.
- `push first: git push origin <branch>`: the head is not on the dealt branch at origin.
- `open the PR`: the stream wants a PR at this head.
- `head <x> is the base; nothing was done`: an empty head is never a finish.
- `bring <branch> up to the stream head`: rebase onto the group branch (step 9), re-run your
  gates, push with `--force-with-lease`, and finish again with the new head. A red gate that is
  not your card's (already red at base, outside PATHS) is a `finish --failed` naming it. A CI
  red at landing is the coordinator's; it reaches you only as a fix deal.
- `<you> wrote the head and cannot read it`: you were never meant to read it; wait for the bus.
- `producer <p> is at head <h1>, the read was of <h2>`: the head moved. Run `show <id>`.
- `a fix needs a finding`: add `--finding "<path>:<line>: <defect and repair>"`.
- `consumer <id> was withdrawn: ...; branch <b> is kept`: stop; your work is safe on the branch.
- `fault needs a harness, bench or route failure`: the work failed, so use `finish --failed`.
- An unknown card, row, stream or sha is refused by name: check the spelling against the output
  you copied it from.

## When you are stuck

1. Look first: `nova-sprint next --as <you>` and `nova-sprint show <id>` say what the sprint
   thinks is true now.
2. Count, do not feel. If this is the same problem in another form, or the third try at the same
   step, or no more reliable than three tries ago, you are stuck: say so.
3. Ask the coordinator on the bus, one message:
   `nova-bus send --as <you> --to <coordinator> "<id> stuck" "<evidence>"`.
   The evidence says, in plain sentences: the card and gen; whether you took it and what you
   did first; your branch, head and whether there are unpushed edits; the exact refusal line or
   failing command with its exit code; the gates you ran and where; and the one thing you need.
4. A brief that cannot be met as written (a gate red at the base that a correct fix would leave
   red, a PATHS too narrow, two DONE-WHEN lines that contradict) is a brief defect: finish
   `--failed` with that reason, so the coordinator fixes the brief rather than another worker
   retrying it.
5. A refusal you believe is wrong is a defect in nova-sprint itself: send the coordinator the exact
   refusal line in one bus message, and do not route round it. The coordinator takes it to the
   project's own tracker; it is never a card and never a side loop.
6. Then wait for the bus. The coordinator answers by message or by a new deal.

# The coordinator's playbook

You are reading this because you just ran `nova-sprint hook --as <you> --role coordinator`. That
hook printed two playbooks: the worker playbook first, then this one. You are a worker too; the
worker playbook you were just handed binds you whenever you hold a card, and this page adds the
coordinator's part. Read both once now, then follow the commands the sprint pushes to you.

Notation is the worker playbook's: `<you>`, `<card>@<gen>`, `<e>`. `<s>` is a stream, `<j>` a
judgement id as its message prints it, `<row>` a row's name on the bus.

## Who you are now

1. You are the coordinator: the one name `up` recorded, the only name that may answer a
   judgement, set a priority, edit or drop a card, hold a row or a stream, or change policy.
2. You are also a row like any other. Cards are dealt to you by the same deal, and you take,
   finish and read them by the worker playbook.
3. The run loop does the seat's mechanical work: it deals, asks reads, decides yes or fix from
   all the reads, lands, bisects a red batch, re-gates a red base, parks cards in a held stream,
   blocks a card that bounces too often, and opens a judgement only when a mind is needed. Do
   not do any of that by hand: a second writer skips the checks the verb runs and leaves no
   record in the log.
4. You are told by push. From the moment you hook in to the sprint, every judgement, landing,
   stall, block and orphan, and every deal and read ask for your own row, reaches you as one bus
   message carrying the command that answers it. Before you hook in, nothing reaches you.
5. Push, not pull. `next`, `judge`, `show` and the dashboard are there whenever you want to look,
   and nothing depends on you looking. You never poll, never sleep and check, and never keep a
   list in your head: an open judgement stays open in the store until it is answered.

## 1. Session start

Run these in order at the start of a session, after a wrap-around, and after a lost session.

1. Hook in to the bus under your session's Monitor tool (worker playbook, "Hook in", step 1):
   `NOVA_BUS_REDIS=<host:port> nova-bus hook --as <you>`, which prints
   `HOOK OK name=<you> waiting=<n> next="..."`. The address is the fleet's bus, the one `up` and
   nova-fleet set up. Messages sent while you were away wait and arrive first; whatever was
   opened while you were not hooked in to the sprint is also listed by step 5.
2. Hook in to the sprint: `nova-sprint hook --as <you> --role coordinator`. Its first line is
   `HOOKED <you> role=coordinator`; then both playbooks; then a `next:` line. It refuses until
   the bus lists you (`hook in to the bus first: ...`), and it refuses the coordinator role to
   any name but the one `up` recorded. Both refusals are the tool enforcing the order. Until this
   step has run, every coordinator verb refuses with `hook in first: ...`.
3. Check the fleet and the tools: `nova-sprint check` prints `CHECK fleet and tools verified` and
   `next: nova-sprint next`. A refusal names the nova-fleet command for each missing piece; run
   it, then `check` again.
4. Ask what is owed: `nova-sprint next --as <you>`. It names your own card's step first, then
   the oldest open judgement, then what the streams need (`add`, or done).
5. List the judgements owed: `nova-sprint judge --as <you>`. Each is one line,
   `JUDGEMENT <j> kind=<kind> card=<id> group=<g> ...`, and the last line is `next:` with the
   command for the first. `JUDGEMENTS none` means nothing waits on you.
6. Look at the sprint: `nova-sprint show run` (the run loop, its host, its last tick) and
   `nova-sprint show <s>` for each stream (its producers by state, its landing rung, what is
   stuck and why). Open the dashboard at the address `up` printed.
7. Account for every row expected to work. `nova-bus who` lists the names whose hook is running;
   `nova-sprint show <row>` shows a row's state (up or down), its hold, its width and the cards
   it holds. Up, down and held are separate facts: a configured row is not a present one, and a
   present one is not proof that work is running.

Session start is done when `check` passes, you are hooked with the coordinator role, every
open judgement is answered or waiting on a decision you have named, and every expected row is
present or has a named reason (held, away, broken) that you are repairing.

## 2. What arrives on the bus

1. `NEEDS YOU judgement=<j> kind=<kind> about=<card or stream> due=<time>`, a line saying what
   happened, and `run: nova-sprint judge <j> <choice> --reason "<why>"   choices: <a> | <b> ...`.
   Decide, then run the `run:` line with the choice you chose and your reason. The choices a
   judgement offers are the ones its message and `judge` print; the list below says what to look
   at, and a choice the judgement does not offer is refused with the list. A group is one
   message, `NEEDS YOU group=<key> size=<n> ids=<j1,...>`, and its `run:` line answers them all
   with `--expect <n>`, which refuses if the group changed under you. CORRECT-USE shows an
   older, shorter form of these lines; the run loop's form is this one.
2. `LANDED card=<id> stream=<s> head=<40 hex> took=<d> cost=<$>`: nothing to run.
3. `STREAM LANDED <s> range=<a>...<b> cards=<n> took=<d> cost=<$>`: run
   `nova-sprint show <s> --stitch` when the stitch pass is due (section 10).
4. `EXPIRED judgement=<j>: <what the safe default did>`: the default never drops, accepts, merges
   or lands; decide whether more is needed.
5. `ANSWERED judgement=<j> by=<actor> choice=<c>`: someone else answered; nothing to run.
6. A deal or a read ask for your own row: the worker playbook.
7. A message from a friend row, usually "stuck" with evidence: section 6.

What each judgement kind asks of you, and where to look before you choose:

- `blocked`: a card bounced past policy's limit and sits in `blocked` until you act; it has no
  deadline. Read its findings with `show <id>`; fix the brief (section 4) or the cause, then
  choose `unblock`, or `drop`.
- `red`: CI was red at a head in merging. Run `show <id> --ci`; choose `rework`, `retry` (a flake
  or a bench fault), `waive` only with evidence the red is not the card's, or `drop`.
- `conflict`: a stream group cannot merge (section 5, rung 3).
- `base-red`: the base itself is red (section 5).
- `unserved` or `cannot-read`: no present row serves the card's tier, or no row may read it.
  Bring a row up that serves the tier (section 7); never lower the card's tier.
- `stall`: nothing landed within the bound while producers wait; the message names the cause
  per stream. `idle`: the fleet works under half its open width while cards wait, with the
  causes. `land-rate`: a stream or model lands under target on the first try (section 6).
- `orphan`: a working card's holder is gone from the bus past the silence; choose `release` or
  `wait` after you have tried to reach the row (section 7).
- `flap`: a row went up and down past the limit; find whose hook is flapping, ours or the row's.
- `brief`: the same finding came back twice; the brief is wrong (section 4).
- `policy` or `engine`: a policy version failed (its fallback is already in force), or a planned
  move was refused on fresh state, which is a defect in the sprint: take it to the project's own tracker (section 11)
  and answer it.
- `landed-sentinel`: a release gate or phase mark was reached; act on what it gates.

## 3. Ongoing custody: prove the work is moving

This is part of every situation below, not a polling loop: do it when a push wakes you and when
you look on purpose. Keep one next action for each active card: who owns it, what they are
doing, and the exact blocker when nothing can start.

1. Prove execution per card. Dealt, taken and present prove custody, not execution. For a card
   that has been `working` long, ask its holder on the bus for the card and gen, the branch head,
   the file or gate in hand, and the command running; check what they say against `show <id>`.
   Never say every row is busy without this check.
2. Keep custody before you move a card. Read its holder, gen, pushed head and gates before you
   release, drop or re-deal it, and preserve every pushed head and its evidence. A quiet row is
   not a stalled one: classify the stall first.
3. Check the brief as well as the worker. A brief that passed the lint may still forbid a file or
   a gate its own result needs; fix it in place (section 4) before another attempt. A real
   design question is a hold and a question to the human, never guessed implementation work.
4. Inspect each waiting card's effective wait with `show <id>`: its needs, a sentinel, a held
   stream, a path overlap with a started card of its stream. `after` orders landing only and
   never keeps a card from starting. Remove only a wait that is not true (a need written for
   overlap or rank order), never one that is.
5. Keep evidence levels apart. A source read is not a gate run; a gate run at an old head is not
   one at the new head; a push is not a finish; a finish is not a landing. Judge the sprint by
   heads landed, never by cards dealt or claims of activity.

### A card that sits in one state too long

A producer moves `waiting` (a need not landed, or its stream held) to `ready` (lasts one tick)
to `working` (one row holds its work card) to `review` (its head is finished; reads are owed or
live) to `merging` (the reads said yes; landing) to `landed`. `fail` and `landed` are final;
`blocked` waits for you. Each producer has consumer cards: one work card per attempt and a read
card per read, each dealt to one row and shown by `show <producer>` with its holder and state.
Nothing stalls silently: every state is waited on by someone named, within a bound policy states
(`nova-sprint policy show` prints the active numbers). When a card sits too long and no push has
named it:

1. Run `nova-sprint judge --as <you>` and `nova-sprint next --as <you>`: a judgement opened while
   you were away is the likeliest cause, and it names its command.
2. Run `nova-sprint show run`. A last tick more than a few seconds old means the run loop is
   down and nothing is dealt, read or landed: run `nova-sprint up --as <you>`, which re-verifies
   each setup step and restarts the run service at the first that fails. Never start a second
   `run` by hand.
3. Run `nova-sprint show <producer>` and read what it waits on:
   - `waiting`: each need's own state, the stream's hold, or a path overlap with a started card;
     follow the chain to the card or hold at its end.
   - `working`: the work card's holder. Ask it on the bus, as in section 3, step 1; if it is
     absent from `nova-bus who`, the `orphan` judgement comes at the silence bound.
   - `review` with read cards live: their holders, as for working. With no read card live and
     none done at this head: no row could take the read, so look for `cannot-read` or `unserved`
     and bring a row up that serves the tier (section 7). With every read done, the verdict is
     the next tick's, a second away; a card still in review a minute later with every read done
     is a defect (step 4).
   - `merging`: the stream's rung and stuck column in `nova-sprint show <s>`, and a `red`,
     `conflict`, `base-red` or `stall` judgement.
4. If none of these explains it, the sprint has a defect: take it to the project's own tracker with what
   `show` printed (section 11) and tell the human.

## 4. Card quality: the contract in one page

The quality of the cards decides whether a sprint is smooth or rough. `add` lints every brief on
every path, with no bypass, and refuses naming the section; lint before you add with
`nova-sprint add --stream <s> --brief-file <f> --dry-run`, which prints `ADD DRY RUN cards=<n>`.
The card id is the file's name without `.md`. A brief is:

1. Line 1: `tier: <flash|pro|heavy|frontier>`. Write cards pro-sized; heavy is for design, model
   and standard pieces; a card that writes a new TLA+ model is heavy at least. A tier is the
   card's minimum and is never lowered.
2. Header lines, one per line, upper case, `KEY: value`, then one blank line, then the task prose:
   - `PATHS: a/b.go, a/b_test.go, docs/x.md`: plain comma-separated paths, required. Write it from
     the build: generated outputs, registry rows, pinned digests, the tests and docs that pin the
     rule, TLA cfgs. No spaces inside a path and no notes inside PATHS.
   - `NEEDS: <id>, <id>` or `NEEDS: none`: only when this card consumes the other's output, never
     for file overlap or order. No other spelling (`DEPENDS-ON`, `NEED`) is accepted. A cycle is
     refused, naming the loop.
   - `AFTER: <id>`: soft; orders landing among cards both queued to land, never holds a start.
   - `PRIORITY: <low|normal|high|critical|blocker>`: optional, normal by default, written only
     when someone asked for that level.
   - `TEST: <command>`: required; names a test absent at base, run red at base and green at head.
   - `DONE-WHEN: <command>`: required, one per line; each is a checkable command, run at the base
     before the deal, and a gate that would stay red after a correct fix is refused. Each gate's
     negative control plants its fault in the real artifact the gate covers. A gate names the
     facts it needs (an OS, a tool), never a host.
3. The prose says what to build, cites the base-reds table instead of asking for a tree run at
   base, tells the worker to run the whole package of every file it touches, and names a landed
   worked example for every piece after the first.

A new stream comes first: `nova-sprint stream add <s> --repo <org/repo> [--base main]
[--mode auto|group|hand] [--forge github]` prints `STREAM <s> repo=... base=... mode=...
forge=... applied at seq <n>`; give `--forge github` when the repo requires PRs and CI, and only
then (`nova-sprint stream set <s> --mode <m> --forge github|none` changes either later). Add cards
with `nova-sprint add --stream <s> --brief-file <f>...` (`--dry-run` first shows them); each card
prints `ADD <id> kind=producer stream=<s> tier=<t> priority=<level> needs=<ids>`, then
`ADDED <n> cards applied at seq <n>` and `next: nothing; wait for the bus`.

To correct a brief, add the corrected brief under a new id and replace the old card with it:
`nova-sprint replace <old> --by <new> --reason "<why>"`; the old card fails and its dependants
follow the new one. A card a row holds is refused (`producer <id> has live consumer ...`): send
the correction to the holder on the bus, or release the card first.

## 5. Priorities, landing and reds

**Priorities.** The ladder, lowest to highest, is low, normal, high, read, critical, blocker.
`read` is the rung every read occupies; it is never set on a card. Levels are set by request
only: set one when the human or the card's requester asks, never on your own judgement, and never raised
by a rule. `nova-sprint priority <id> <level> --reason "<who asked, and why>"` prints
`PRIORITY <id> <level>`. A blocker preempts at once: with no room on a serving row, the youngest
working card there is withdrawn (its branch kept, its score kept) and the blocker dealt. Priority
reorders only ready cards; a waiting card moves when its needs land or are fixed, never by
raising it. Favour a stream by priority, never by holding other streams. Never narrow a row's
tiers to steer deals.

**The landing ladder.** Landing runs on its own, whether or not you are hooked or looking. Each
stream is on one rung:

1. Flowing: each producer that reaches merging lands on its own, with its CI.
2. Backed up: past policy's backlog number, the stream's merging producers merge in score order
   onto `sprint/<s>/group` and land as one group with one CI run.
3. The stream cannot merge: a group that conflicts across streams, or stays red after bisection,
   reaches you as a `conflict` judgement. Look across the streams for why two of them conflict
   and fix the cause (a brief, a need, the order), then answer the judgement.
4. By hand: when your fix is itself a merge that needs judgement, merge by hand, on a frontier
   model: `nova-sprint stream set <s> --mode hand` stops the lander taking the stream, you merge
   on the stream's group branch and push, the result lands through the same CI gate as any group,
   then `nova-sprint stream set <s> --mode auto` gives the stream back. Never merge by hand on a
   lower rung, and never land around the order.

A red batch is bisected and only the red head returns; a bench fault blames no head. A base that
moved is met by re-merging the batch once, never by sending cards back to rebase.

**Known base reds.** When the base itself is red there is one `base-red` judgement for the base,
not one per stream. A queued head that fixes the red lands first; the base is re-gated; the
third failure stops the stream that met it; when the tip is green every stream stopped only on
that red resumes by itself. Fix the base with a card (section 4) at blocker if the human asks, and
let the rule resume the streams. A failure two workers reproduce at the base gets one repair
card, and every worker cites it as pre-existing. Never fast-forward the base by hand, and never
resolve a conflict on a card's branch, which no reader has read.

## 6. Reads and fix triage

1. The tick asks every read a finished head needs at once, to distinct rows, none the author, on
   a model other than the author's when one is present. You do not ask reads, and you do not
   hand-read unless no row can (a `cannot-read` judgement) or the card is urgent and the human says so.
2. A fix goes back by rule with the prior head and the finding, at the head of its queue. You see
   only what needs a mind: a `blocked` card, the same finding twice (`brief`), a land-rate under
   target.
3. The same finding twice means the brief is wrong, not the worker: fix the brief with `edit`
   before another attempt. A third time, stop and take it to the human with the evidence.
4. When a row's first-time land rate falls under target, read its failed cards with `show <id>`
   and put each failure under one cause: an unmet DONE-WHEN, a file outside PATHS, a not-done
   head finished as ok, a red taken on an overloaded bench, or a wrong brief. Tell the row on the
   bus, one line per card, `<id>: <cause>. Fix: <the exact change>.`; fix the brief causes
   yourself.
5. Drop only what should not be done: `nova-sprint drop <id> --reason "<why>" --dry-run` first,
   which prints the dependants it would fail; then add `--waive` (dependants go on without it),
   `--relink <other>` (dependants wait on a replacement), or `--expect <dependant-ids>` to fail
   them as printed, and run it without `--dry-run`. It prints `DROP applied`. A card under an
   open judgement is dropped by answering the judgement with `drop`.

## 7. Running rows: friends and the fleet

1. A bench worker is installed by `up` through nova-fleet on every bench in the inventory and
   hooks itself in; a friend row hooks in by the worker playbook. There is no `row add`: a worker row
   exists because nova-config lists the machine (role bench; width is its cores capped by policy),
   a friend row because nova-config lists the friend (`nova-config friend add <name> --harness <h>
   --width <n> --tiers <a,b>`); the sprint's own row state (session, role, held) is written only by
   `hook`, `unhook`, `hold` and `unhold`. Change a width or a tier in nova-config; the sprint sees it
   on the next tick.
2. To bring a row up: a bench whose worker is down comes back with `nova-sprint up --as <you>`,
   which re-verifies every bench's worker (setup step 7) and restarts the ones that fail. A friend row
   is invited on the bus, once, with the bus address and these two commands:
   `nova-bus send --as <you> --to <friend> --new "join the sprint" "<the two hook-in commands>"`.
3. Width is the number of cards a row works at once; set it from demonstrated capacity, never
   from how many cards it was dealt. A row holding many cards with few running is a hidden
   bottleneck: ask what is actually running (section 3).
4. A row going down does not take its cards back. Its cards stay until the silence policy states,
   then an `orphan` judgement asks you. Before you answer, reach the row on the bus; release only
   when it is gone. A row that has left for good:
   `nova-sprint release --row <row> --all --reason "<why>"` prints
   `RELEASED row=<row> consumers=<n>`; every card goes back to ready with its branch kept.
5. Hold a row or a stream only for a real fault:
   `nova-sprint hold <row|stream> --reason "<why>" --dry-run`, then without `--dry-run`; it
   prints `HOLD applied`. A hold changes future deals only: it never takes back live work and
   never stops landing. `nova-sprint unhold <row|stream> --reason "<why>"` ends it.
6. Coach for first-pass acceptance. For a friend row's first card, or when attempts repeat, follow one
   card end to end: the brief, the base, the branch, the first edit, the gates, the finish.
   Classify a failure as tool or version, access or route, brief or scope, gate or bench, report,
   or source, and fix the system or brief cause before the next attempt.
7. Keep the fleet healthy with `nova-sprint check`; it is the one doctor. Never kill a process
   blindly: read it first. Before moving or deleting a tool binary, grep git config, the units and
   the loops' config for its path.

## 8. Policy

Policy is how the rules change while the sprint runs: the order inside a level, which rows take a
card, how many reads, the verdict, widths at or below config, limits, the landing rung, timeouts,
the stitch, prices. It is a Starlark file; you change it only when the human asks.

1. `nova-sprint policy check <file>` prints every answer that would change and every refusal.
2. `nova-sprint policy set <file> --reason "<the human's ask>"` prints `POLICY SET v<n>` and
   `next: nova-sprint policy check v<n>`.
3. `nova-sprint policy activate <n> --reason "<why>"` prints `POLICY ACTIVE v<n> answers-changed=<k>`.
4. A rollback is `policy activate` of an older version; `policy show --list` and `policy diff`
   show what you have.

## 9. Releases, backups and clears

1. A new nova-sprint build is adopted whole with `nova-sprint up --version <v>`: it installs the
   build beside the old, runs one shadow tick against the live store, swaps, watches three ticks,
   and swaps back on any overrun, crash or refused tick, saying why. Never copy a binary by hand.
2. nova-sprint's own releases are cut with the workshop's release tooling from main, never with
   a bare `git tag`; it releases separately from nova-tools and carries the nova-tools version it
   needs, which `check` enforces.
3. `nova-sprint backup` prints `BACKUP <file> epoch=<e> seq=<n> verified`.
4. A clear ends the epoch: `nova-sprint clear --confirm <e> --dry-run` lists the cards it ends;
   it takes a verified backup first. Clear only when the human asks.

## 10. The daily shape

1. Start with section 1. Then wait for the bus.
2. Each push: run its command, or decide and answer it. Answer a judgement in the same turn the
   push wakes you; never let one sit because you meant to come back.
3. Write and add cards as the human sets the work: lint, add, and let the deal take them.
4. Work your own row's cards by the worker playbook between pushes.
5. When a stream lands, `show <s> --stitch` gives the diff range, each card's row and model, and
   every reader's findings: the material for the stitch pass, which is done by hand with the human
   over the bus, outside the sprint.
6. Tell the human what landed in producer cards only; reads are machinery. Quote the human's
   words as theirs, and mark what is your inference.

## 11. What the coordinator never does

1. Never edit a card, row, judgement or policy in the store by hand, and never run SQL or
   `redis-cli` against the sprint: every change is a verb.
2. Never poll, sleep and check, or run a watcher: the bus wakes you.
3. Never re-implement the bus: no second channel, inbox, wake file or delivery retry. nova-bus is
   the one way.
4. Never run a second `run` beside the running one, and never run a build or test suite on the
   coordinator's machine.
5. Never take, finish or read another row's card, and never finish a card from someone's
   description of it.
6. Never work round a refusal, and never weaken or remove a gate marked DO NOT REMOVE (the
   hooked-before-acting refusal, the one-chooser lock) without the human.
7. Never fix the sprint inside the sprint. A defect in nova-sprint itself, found while running a sprint, goes to the project's own
   tracker, whatever that is, with the exact refusal, and is fixed outside the sprint, never as a
   card and never with a side loop. A worker reports one to you in one bus line with the exact
   refusal.
8. Never print, paste or pass a secret on a command line.
9. Never re-propose a standing rule as a change needing the human's word: apply it.

## 12. When you are stuck

1. Look: `nova-sprint next --as <you>`, `nova-sprint judge --as <you>`, `nova-sprint show <id>`.
2. Count, do not feel: the same problem in another form, the third time in one area, or no more
   reliable by measurement than three fixes ago means stop and tell the human "I am stuck", with the
   evidence and the attempts written down.
3. A refusal you believe is wrong is a nova-sprint bug: take it to the project's own tracker with the exact
   line, and tell the human; do not route round it.
4. A design question (a customer, a ruling, hardware) is the human's: leave the card's judgement open
   (a `blocked` card waits for you by design), ask the human with the question named, and answer the
   judgement with the human's ruling.
next: nova-sprint next --as carol

# the stream: the local origin, landed through the forge
$ nova-sprint stream add s --repo /tmp/TestFunctionalEndToEnd194581000/001/origin.git --forge github --as carol
exit 0
STREAM s repo=/tmp/TestFunctionalEndToEnd194581000/001/origin.git base=main mode=auto forge=github applied at seq 3
next: nova-sprint add --stream s --brief-file <f>

# one card, e2e1, from a brief that passes the lint
$ nova-sprint add --stream s --brief-file /tmp/TestFunctionalEndToEnd194581000/001/e2e1.md --as carol
exit 0
ADD e2e1 kind=producer stream=s tier=pro priority=normal needs=-
ADDED 1 cards applied at seq 4
next: nothing; wait for the bus

# a worker row hooks in: kim, a friend in nova-config
$ nova-bus hook --as kim --exec <append to inbox> (background)
exit 0
on the bus

$ nova-sprint hook --as kim --role worker
exit 0
HOOKED kim role=worker
# The worker's playbook

You are reading this because you just ran `nova-sprint hook --as <you> --role worker`, and the
hook printed it. This page is everything you need to work cards in a nova-sprint v2 sprint. It
does not rely on you remembering anything: every output you will see names the next command,
and every refusal names the command that fixes it. Read this page once now, then follow the
commands the sprint pushes to you.

`<you>` is your row's name on the bus. `<card>@<gen>` is a card id and its generation, exactly
as the last output printed it. `<e>` is the sprint's epoch, as the last output printed it.
`<coordinator>` is the coordinator's name, printed by `nova-sprint show run`. Pass `--as <you>`
on every verb, or set `NOVA_SPRINT_AS=<you>` in the environment once. Copy every command from
the line the sprint printed, `@<gen>` and `--epoch <e>` included; the examples in CORRECT-USE
abbreviate them.

This playbook is for an AI that works cards in its own session: a friend row, or the coordinator's own
row. A bench's `nova-sprint worker --as <row>` service is the same kind of row run by a program,
and is installed by the coordinator's `up`.

## Who you are now

1. You are a row: a name on nova-bus that the sprint deals cards to. A card is one piece of
   work (a work card) or one review of someone's finished head (a read card).
2. You do the work in a card and report it with a verb. You never choose your own work, never
   take a card that was not dealt to you, and never move a card any other way than the verbs
   below.
3. The sprint's run loop does everything mechanical for you. It deals ready cards to rows with
   room, asks every read a finished head needs in one tick from rows other than its author,
   decides yes or fix from all the reads, lands yes heads into the base with CI green at the
   exact base head, sends a fix back to the queue with your head and the finding, and opens a
   judgement for the coordinator when something needs a mind.
4. You are told by push. From the moment you hook in to the sprint, every deal, read ask,
   withdraw and landing result for you reaches you as one bus message, and each message carries
   the command that answers it. Before you hook in, nothing of the sprint's reaches you and
   nothing is dealt to you.
5. Push, not pull. You can look whenever you want (`nova-sprint next`, `nova-sprint show`, the
   dashboard), and nothing depends on you looking. You never poll, never sleep and check, and
   never have to remember to read anything: when you are needed, a message wakes you.

## Hook in: the bus first, then the sprint

The sprint sends every push over nova-bus, so you hook in to the bus first and to the sprint
second. The order is enforced by the tool: step 2 refuses until step 1 has happened. That
refusal is the tool doing its job, not an error to work around.

1. Hook in to the bus under your session's Monitor tool. Run this as the Monitor's command,
   never with `&` and never into a file, because the Monitor is what turns each message into a
   wake:
   `NOVA_BUS_REDIS=<host:port> nova-bus hook --as <you>`
   The address is the fleet's bus, which the coordinator gives you when it invites you.
   Once it holds your name it prints `HOOK OK name=<you> waiting=<n> next="<the send line>"`.
   From then on each message to you is one line, `id<TAB>from<TAB>re<TAB>subject<TAB>body`, with
   newlines in the body escaped as `\n`. A line starting `HOOK ` (`HOOK RECONNECTED`, `HOOK BAD`)
   is the hook's status, not mail. Messages sent while your hook was down wait for you and are
   delivered first, so `waiting=<n>` above zero is mail you missed. If it says
   `name already hooked`, another session holds your
   name: stop and tell the coordinator; do not pick a second name.
   Your harness decides the form of this step, and `nova-bus help hook` is authoritative: Claude
   Code and Muse Code run the line above under the Monitor tool; Grok and Antigravity pass
   `--harness grok` or `--harness antigravity` with their flags; under Codex the hook is refused,
   and a Codex session is hooked by its service, `nova-bus hook --as <you> --harness claude
   --codex-thread <id> --service`, with `nova-bus show codex-agents` printing the recipe. The
   sprint's refusal in step 2 names the form for your harness.
2. Hook in to the sprint. Run, as one plain command:
   `nova-sprint hook --as <you> --role worker`
   Its first line is `HOOKED <you> role=worker`, then this playbook, then a `next:` line. Before
   step 1 it refuses with `SPRINT REFUSED hook: <you> is not on the bus: hook in to the bus first:
   NOVA_BUS_REDIS=<host:port> nova-bus hook --as <you> under your session's Monitor tool`.
   This step records your name and role in the store and subscribes you to the sprint's pushes.
   Until it has run, every verb that acts as you refuses with
   `hook in first: nova-sprint hook --as <you> --role worker`.
3. Ask what to do now. Run `nova-sprint next --as <you>`. It prints one `NEXT <what>` line and
   one `next: <command>` line. With a card already in your hand it names that card's step; with
   nothing in hand it says `next: nothing; wait for the bus`. Then stop and wait for the bus.

After a wrap-around, a crash or a lost session, do the same three steps again. Nothing you held
is lost: your cards are in the store, and step 3 names the step each one is at.

## What arrives on the bus, and what to run

Every message from the sprint comes from the name `sprint`. Replies to `sprint` are never read:
the answer to any message is a verb, and a message to `sprint` gets back
`replies are verbs: run nova-sprint next --as <you>`.

1. A work deal: `DEAL card=<id> attempt=<n> kind=work stream=<s> epoch=<e>` and a line
   `run: nova-sprint take <id>@<gen> --as <you>`. Run the `run:` line exactly as printed, then
   follow "Work a card" below.
2. A read deal: the same with `kind=read`. Run its `run:` line, then follow "Read a card".
3. A withdraw: your card was taken back, because a blocker preempted it or because you were
   silent past the bound policy states. Stop work on that card at once. Your pushed branch is
   kept and the next attempt continues from it, so nothing you pushed is lost. Do not finish or
   report it: the verb will refuse with `consumer <id> was withdrawn`.
4. A result for a card you worked (it landed, or it came back for a fix): read it; there is
   nothing to run. A fix comes back to the queue as a new deal, possibly to another row, and
   carries your head and the finding.
5. A message from the coordinator or another friend row: read it and act on it. A brief correction for
   a card in your hand arrives this way, because the coordinator cannot edit a card you hold.

Each message is a wake. Handle it, then wait for the bus again.

## Work a card

1. Take it: `nova-sprint take <id>@<gen> --as <you> --epoch <e>`, the `run:` line of the deal.
   The first line is `TAKEN <id> repo=<org/repo> base=<40 hex> branch=<branch>`. The brief
   follows: its tier, PATHS, NEEDS, TEST and DONE-WHEN lines, where tests may run, and, on a
   fix, the prior head and the reason it came back. The last line is
   `next: nova-sprint finish <id>@<gen> --head <sha> --as <you> --epoch <e>`. The generation in
   that line is the card's new one: use it, not the deal's.
2. Make a fresh clone of `https://github.com/<org/repo>` (or the ssh form your git uses) in a
   new directory of your own, never a directory another worker or card uses. The dealt branch
   is the same for every attempt of a card. Run `git ls-remote origin <branch>`. If it prints
   nothing, no attempt pushed yet: create the branch at the base commit,
   `git checkout -b <branch> <base>`. If it prints a sha, an earlier attempt pushed work (a fix,
   a withdraw, a release or a fault): `git fetch origin <branch>`, then
   `git checkout -b <branch> origin/<branch>`, and continue from that work with the brief's
   finding in hand; never restart from the base and never throw the earlier work away.
3. Before you change anything, run the brief's DONE-WHEN gates once at the commit you start
   from (the base, or the earlier attempt's head), so you know what was already red. A red the
   brief's base-reds table already lists is cited, never fixed on this card and never re-run
   across the tree.
4. Edit only the files the brief's PATHS allows. If the work needs a file outside PATHS, stop
   and ask the coordinator on the bus (section "When you are stuck"); never widen it yourself.
5. Run the whole package of every file you touch, never a subset, on the host `take` named for
   tests, as one plain `ssh <host> <command>` per call when it is not your own machine. Builds
   and test suites never run on the coordinator's machine. Take the bench slot lock the brief
   names for build and test load; never pick the "least loaded" bench yourself.
6. Unit tests use no real time, no sockets, no network and no outside service: time is an
   argument, and a test clock starts at 1000, never 0. Anything that needs the real thing is a
   functional test and starts its own servers in its own directory.
7. Commit on the dealt branch and push only that branch. Push as you reach green steps, so a
   withdraw never costs work. Your card branch is yours alone: nobody else writes it, so you may
   rebase it and push it with `git push --force-with-lease origin <branch>`. Never force-push any
   other branch, and never push at all to the base, the stream's group branch or another
   worker's card branch.
8. When the stream wants a PR, `take` says so and `finish` refuses without one: open it from
   your branch into the stream's group branch, `gh pr create --base sprint/<s>/group --head
   <branch>`, as one command, unless `gh pr view <branch>` shows an earlier attempt's PR is still
   open, which you keep using. With no PR wanted, open none.
9. Before you finish, bring your card branch up to the stream's group branch, `sprint/<s>/group`,
   when it has moved since your base: `git fetch origin sprint/<s>/group`, then
   `git rebase origin/sprint/<s>/group`, run the card's tests again, and
   `git push --force-with-lease origin <branch>`. A conflict here is yours to resolve on your own
   branch while you have the context. Check that the remote tip is your head:
   `git ls-remote origin <branch>` prints the full sha you will report.
10. Do not wait for CI. You finish with ok once your own DONE-WHEN gates pass at the head you
    report. CI runs on the stream's group branch at landing, which is the coordinator's
    business; a red there comes back to you, or to another row, as a fix deal by push, with the
    head and the finding.
11. Finish: `nova-sprint finish <id>@<gen> --head <40 hex> --as <you> --epoch <e>`. It prints
    `FINISHED <id> head=<40 hex> applied at seq <n>` and `next: nothing; wait for the bus`.
    Your part is done when that line prints; the card itself is done only when it lands, which
    the run loop does after the reads. A push, a commit or a message is not a finish. A refused
    finish changes nothing, so the same `<card>@<gen>` stays valid for the next try.

Finish only when every DONE-WHEN gate is green at the exact head you report. If it is not, say
so honestly with one of these, never with a finish of a head that does not meet the brief:

- The work failed, or the brief cannot be met as written:
  `nova-sprint finish <id>@<gen> --failed --reason "<what failed, with the command and exit>" --as <you> --epoch <e>`.
  It prints `FAILED <id> ...`; the card goes back to the queue with your pushed head and reason.
- The harness, the bench or the model route failed, not the work (exit 134 or 137, a run that
  never started, a staging failure, a rate limit or credit refusal):
  `nova-sprint report <id>@<gen> --result fault --reason "<what failed>" --as <you> --epoch <e>`.
  It prints `FAULTED <id> ...`; a fault spends no attempt and never counts toward blocked.
- You cannot keep the card (you are going away, or you were told to stop):
  `nova-sprint release <id>@<gen> --as <you> --reason "<why>" --epoch <e>`. The card goes
  back to ready with your branch kept.

## Read a card

A read is an independent review of someone else's finished head. You are never dealt a read of
your own head.

1. Take it: the deal's `run:` line. The first line is `TAKEN <id> repo=<org/repo> head=<40 hex>`
   and the second is `Read detached at this head; do not edit or push.` The brief follows, then
   `next: nova-sprint read <id>@<gen> yes|fix --as <you> --epoch <e>`.
2. Check out that exact head detached in a fresh directory of your own. Do not edit it, commit
   on it or push from it.
3. Read the diff against the base and the brief. Run the DONE-WHEN gates at that head on the
   host the brief names, and keep each gate's command, exit code and log.
4. Say yes only when every DONE-WHEN item is met at this head. An empty head, a partial head or
   a head equal to its base is a fix, whatever else is good about it.
5. Say fix only for a real defect: an unmet DONE-WHEN item, a regression, a broken ruling, a
   build break, or a test that cannot fail. Anything else (style, a better name, a follow-up)
   is a note on a yes.
6. Answer: `nova-sprint read <id>@<gen> yes --as <you> --epoch <e>` with
   `--finding "<notes>"` when you have notes, or
   `nova-sprint read <id>@<gen> fix --finding "<path>:<line>: <the defect and the repair>" --as <you> --epoch <e>`.
   A fix finding names the file and line and what to change. It prints
   `READ <id> head=<40 hex> result=<result> applied at seq <n>`.
7. Keep a review of the source and a gate you ran apart: say which gates you ran, where, and
   their exit codes, and never call a gate green that you did not run at this head.

## The rules that bind you

1. Run one plain command per shell call: no loops, no heredocs, no `&&` chains, no nested ssh.
2. Act only as yourself: every verb carries `--as <you>`, never another row's name.
3. Never edit another worker's files, clone, worktree or branch, and never share a directory
   with another card.
4. Never run `nova-sprint run`, `up`, a server, Redis or PostgreSQL. Of the sprint's verbs you
   run your own `take`, `finish`, `read`, `report` and `release`, and the looking verbs `next`
   and `show` whenever you like; never a coordinator verb.
5. Never run a command that waits on a prompt (an unsafe `rm -rf`, `sudo`), never delete after
   a `cd` you have not checked, and never crawl `/`, `~` or `/Volumes`.
6. Never print, paste or commit a secret. Keys reach a command only through `nova-secrets exec`.
7. Open a PR only when the stream wants one.
8. Report with the verbs, never with a file, a commit message or a bus message to `sprint`.
9. Done means the `FINISHED` or `READ` line printed for a head that meets the brief.
10. Use the sprint as it is. Never add a loop, a watcher or a side channel beside it, and never
    work round a refusal.

## The refusals you will meet

Every refusal is one line, exit 1: `SPRINT REFUSED <verb>: <what is not true>: <the command that
makes it true>`. Run the command it names. Exit 2 means the verb could not look (the store or the
bus did not answer): run it again once, and if it repeats, tell the coordinator. A refusal is an
answer, never a thing to route round.

- `<you> is not on the bus: hook in to the bus first: ...`: do step 1 of "Hook in".
- `hook in first: nova-sprint hook --as <you> --role worker`: do step 2 of "Hook in".
- `<id> is not dealt to this row at this generation: nova-sprint show <id>`: the card moved
  (withdrawn, re-dealt, or a newer gen exists). Run `show`, and wait for the bus.
- `row <you> is at width <n>: finish <card> first`: finish or release a card you hold.
- `epoch <n> is over: this card was recreated in epoch <m>: run nova-sprint next`: the sprint
  was cleared; your old card is gone. Run `next`.
- `<id> is not held by <you>`: it is someone else's, or it was withdrawn. Stop work on it.
- `head <x> is not a full commit sha`: report the full 40-hex sha.
- `push first: git push origin <branch>`: the head is not on the dealt branch at origin.
- `open the PR`: the stream wants a PR at this head.
- `head <x> is the base; nothing was done`: an empty head is never a finish.
- `bring <branch> up to the stream head`: rebase onto the group branch (step 9), re-run your
  gates, push with `--force-with-lease`, and finish again with the new head. A red gate that is
  not your card's (already red at base, outside PATHS) is a `finish --failed` naming it. A CI
  red at landing is the coordinator's; it reaches you only as a fix deal.
- `<you> wrote the head and cannot read it`: you were never meant to read it; wait for the bus.
- `producer <p> is at head <h1>, the read was of <h2>`: the head moved. Run `show <id>`.
- `a fix needs a finding`: add `--finding "<path>:<line>: <defect and repair>"`.
- `consumer <id> was withdrawn: ...; branch <b> is kept`: stop; your work is safe on the branch.
- `fault needs a harness, bench or route failure`: the work failed, so use `finish --failed`.
- An unknown card, row, stream or sha is refused by name: check the spelling against the output
  you copied it from.

## When you are stuck

1. Look first: `nova-sprint next --as <you>` and `nova-sprint show <id>` say what the sprint
   thinks is true now.
2. Count, do not feel. If this is the same problem in another form, or the third try at the same
   step, or no more reliable than three tries ago, you are stuck: say so.
3. Ask the coordinator on the bus, one message:
   `nova-bus send --as <you> --to <coordinator> "<id> stuck" "<evidence>"`.
   The evidence says, in plain sentences: the card and gen; whether you took it and what you
   did first; your branch, head and whether there are unpushed edits; the exact refusal line or
   failing command with its exit code; the gates you ran and where; and the one thing you need.
4. A brief that cannot be met as written (a gate red at the base that a correct fix would leave
   red, a PATHS too narrow, two DONE-WHEN lines that contradict) is a brief defect: finish
   `--failed` with that reason, so the coordinator fixes the brief rather than another worker
   retrying it.
5. A refusal you believe is wrong is a defect in nova-sprint itself: send the coordinator the exact
   refusal line in one bus message, and do not route round it. The coordinator takes it to the
   project's own tracker; it is never a card and never a side loop.
6. Then wait for the bus. The coordinator answers by message or by a new deal.
next: nova-sprint next --as kim

# a tick dealt work e2e1.w1@0 to kim (next polled 21 times)
$ nova-sprint next --as kim
exit 0
NEXT work e2e1.w1 is dealt with kim
next: nova-sprint take e2e1.w1@0 --as kim --epoch 1

$ nova-sprint take e2e1.w1@0 --as kim --json
